segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to look at the tomb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And suddenly there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord came down from heaven, approached, rolled away the stone, and sat on it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing was white as snow.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The guards quaked for fear of him and became like dead men.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the angel said to the women,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “As for you, do not be afraid, for I know that you are looking for Jesus, who was crucified.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: He is not here, for he has been raised, just as he said. Come, see the place where he was lying.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: Then go quickly and tell his disciples, ‘He has been raised from the dead, and look, he is going ahead of you to Galilee; there you will see him.’ Look, I have told you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they left the tomb quickly, with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And suddenly Jesus met them and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Greetings!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came up, took hold of his feet, and bowed down before him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not be afraid. Go and tell my brothers to leave for Galilee, and there they will see me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While they were on their way, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests everything that had happened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The chief priests met with the elders and, after forming a plan, gave the soldiers a large sum of silver,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: telling them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Say, ‘His disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will persuade him and see that you have nothing to worry about.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they took the silver and did as they had been instructed. And this story has been spread among Jews to this very day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had directed them to go,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when they saw him they bowed down before him, but some doubted.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus came up and spoke to them, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Go, therefore, and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: teaching them to keep all that I have commanded you. And look, I am with you all the days, until the end of the age.”

notes.traditional: In the end of the sabbath / After the Sabbath
notes.note: The Greek word usually means "late", which would give "late on the Sabbath". In this period it could also work as a preposition meaning "after". Most scholars take it that way here, since the next phrase places the scene at dawn on the first day of the week. A minority think Matthew reckons the day as ending at sunset, so that the scene is Saturday evening as the new day "draws on".
The verb is the one from which the word for "earthquake" in verse 2 is formed. "Quaked" keeps the echo: the earth shakes, and so do the guards.

The Greek verb is passive in form. It can be read as a true passive ("he has been raised", with God as the implied agent) or as an intransitive ("he has risen"). Both are defensible. The passive is used here and in verse 7 because the New Testament regularly speaks of God raising Jesus.

This was the ordinary everyday Greek greeting. Its literal sense is "rejoice", and some hear that overtone here after the "great joy" of verse 8. A first-century reader would have heard it first as a plain "hello".

The verb names a physical act: prostrating oneself before a superior, whether a king or a god. Here it accompanies grasping Jesus's feet. "Worshiped" is the traditional rendering, and many scholars think Matthew intends full religious devotion in this chapter, given the claim to all authority in verse 18. The rendering keeps the concrete gesture the Greek describes and leaves its significance to the context.

The Greek is literally "if this is heard before the governor". It may mean simply that the report reaches him, or more formally that the matter comes up for a hearing in his court. For a soldier, sleeping on watch was a serious offence, which is why the priests promise protection.

The Greek has no article. It says the story circulated "among Jews", not that it was the view of "the Jews" as a whole. Most translations supply "the". Matthew, himself writing from within a Jewish setting, is describing a report current in his own day.

The Greek can be read as "but some doubted" (part of the group) or "but they doubted" (the same eleven who bowed down). Most translations take the first reading. The verb suggests hesitation or wavering rather than settled disbelief. Its only other New Testament use is of Peter on the water in Matthew 14:31.

The same Greek word is translated "Gentiles" elsewhere, when the non-Jewish peoples are meant. Some scholars read this verse as "all the Gentiles", extending the earlier mission to Israel. Most take the phrase to mean all peoples without distinction, Israel included, and that is the reading followed here.

The Greek preposition is literally "into". Some scholars take the phrase to mean a transfer into the ownership or allegiance of the one named, a sense the expression can have in commercial documents of the period. Others note that "into" and "in" were often interchangeable in Greek of this period. The traditional "in the name" is kept, but the stronger sense is possible.

The Greek says literally "all the days", a Semitic way of saying "always". It is kept because it completes a fourfold repetition in Jesus's closing words: all authority, all the nations, all that I have commanded, all the days.

candidates.reason: It recurs across the Gospels, Acts, Paul, Hebrews and Revelation, and the choice between "worship", "bow down" and "pay homage" carries christological weight that should not vary chapter by chapter.
This very frequent attention marker is rendered "behold", "look", "suddenly" or dropped by different translators, and needs a policy for narrative as against direct speech.
The passive forms used of Jesus's resurrection can be "was raised" or "rose", and the choice should be uniform across the Gospels, Acts and Paul.
